direct_answer: Insoles and orthotics may help some people with foot or ankle pain. Evidence for knee osteoarthritis is limited. A podiatrist or physiotherapist can assess you, and insoles need shoes with room for them.
author: Louis Maxwell

content:
Insoles are widely sold but do not suit everyone.

This guide covers what to know. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

Who might benefit

Some people with foot or ankle pain.

Getting assessed

A podiatrist or physiotherapist can advise.

Footwear

Shoes need depth and a removable insole.

Limits

Insoles are not routinely recommended for knee OA.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Can I buy off the shelf?

Some people do; get advice first.

Are they on the NHS?

Sometimes after assessment.

Sources and further reading

  • NHS: Foot pain
  • NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s
